title: Rearranging formulas
goals: Say what each letter in a formula stands for, and what the formula says
Change the subject of a formula by undoing its operations in reverse order
Rearrange formulas with fractions, squares, square roots and brackets
Use a rearranged formula to work out a value, such as a current from Ohm's law
summary:
The **subject** of a formula is the letter on its own on one side: in $V = IR$ it is $V$. **Changing the subject** turns the formula round to give the letter you want.

It is the same fact written another way. $3 \times 4 = 12$ also means $12 \div 4 = 3$. So $V = IR$ also means $I = \frac{V}{R}$ and $R = \frac{V}{I}$.

**The method**

- List what was done to the letter you want, in order.
- Undo each job in **reverse** order, doing the same to **both sides**.
- Opposites: add and take away; times and divide; square and square root.

**A letter on the bottom** of a fraction: multiply both sides by it first. $v = \frac{d}{t}$ gives $vt = d$, then $t = \frac{d}{v}$.

**Pulse-echo**: $d = \frac{vt}{2}$. Undo the halving (times 2), then the times $v$: $t = \frac{2d}{v}$. For the speed, $v = \frac{2d}{t}$.

**Squares**: $P = I^2R$. Divide by $R$, then square root: $I = \sqrt{\frac{P}{R}}$. The area of a circle, $A = \pi r^2$, gives $r = \sqrt{\frac{A}{\pi}}$.

**Brackets**: $F = \frac{9C}{5} + 32$. The add 32 was done last, so take it off first, then times 5, then divide by 9: $C = \frac{5(F - 32)}{9}$. The bracket says: take the 32 off before anything else.

**Check** with numbers you know: $V = IR$ with 3 A and 4 Ω gives 12 V, so your $R = \frac{V}{I}$ should give $12 \div 3 = 4$ Ω back.

Before you start, ask: is the letter I want already the subject? Then just **substitute**. If not, **rearrange** first.

formulas.name: Ohm's law
formulas.says: The voltage across a resistor is the current through it times its resistance.

formulas.name: Current from Ohm's law
formulas.says: Ohm's law turned round: the current is the voltage divided by the resistance.

formulas.name: Resistance from Ohm's law
formulas.says: Ohm's law turned round: the resistance is the voltage divided by the current.

formulas.name: Electrical power
formulas.says: The power is the voltage times the current.

formulas.name: Current from power
formulas.says: The power formula turned round: the current is the power divided by the voltage.
formulas.example: a 2300 W heater on 230 V: $2300 \div 230 = 10$ A.

formulas.name: Speed
formulas.says: The speed is the distance divided by the time.

formulas.name: Distance from speed and time
formulas.says: The distance is the speed times the time.

formulas.name: Time from distance and speed
formulas.says: The time is the distance divided by the speed.

formulas.name: Depth from the echo time
formulas.says: The depth of a flaw is the speed of sound times the echo time, **halved**, because the sound goes there and back.
symbols: the speed of sound in the metal (mm per µs; steel about 5.92)
the time for the echo to come back (µs, millionths of a second)

formulas.name: Echo time from the depth
formulas.says: The pulse-echo rule turned round: twice the depth (down and back up) divided by the speed.
symbols: the speed of sound (mm per µs)

formulas.name: Speed of sound from a calibration block
formulas.says: The pulse-echo rule turned round for the speed: a block of known thickness and a measured echo time give the speed of sound.
symbols: the speed of sound (mm per µs)
formulas.example: a 25 mm block echoing at 8.45 µs: $50 \div 8.45 \approx 5.92$ mm per µs.

formulas.name: Power turned to heat in a resistor
formulas.says: The power is the current squared (times itself), times the resistance.

formulas.name: Current from power and resistance
formulas.says: $P = I^2R$ turned round: divide the power by the resistance, then take the square root.

formulas.name: Area of a circle
formulas.says: The area inside a circle is pi times the radius squared.
symbols: the area (mm², if the radius is in mm)
the radius: centre to edge, half the diameter

formulas.name: Radius from the area
formulas.says: The area of a circle turned round: divide the area by pi, then take the square root.

formulas.name: Celsius to Fahrenheit
formulas.says: Times the Celsius temperature by 9, divide by 5, then add 32.

formulas.name: Fahrenheit to Celsius
formulas.says: Take 32 off the Fahrenheit temperature, times by 5, then divide by 9.

formulas.name: Pay for the hours you work
formulas.says: Your pay is the hourly rate times the number of hours.

cards.q: Have a go: a guess is fine. **Ohm's law** is $V = IR$: the voltage $V$ (volts) equals the current $I$ (amps) times the resistance $R$ (ohms). Which of these gives the current $I$?
cards.why: Numbers first: $12 = 3 \times 4$ means $3 = 12 \div 4$. In the same way, $V = I \times R$ means $I = V \div R$. $I = VR$ multiplies when you need to divide; $\frac{R}{V}$ divides the wrong way up. Check with 12 V and 4 Ω: $\frac{12}{4} = 3$ A, and $3 \times 4 = 12$.

cards.title: The subject of a formula
cards.body:
A **formula** is a rule linking letters. In **Ohm's law**, $V = IR$:

- $V$ is the voltage, in volts (V)
- $I$ is the current, in amps (A)
- $R$ is the resistance, in ohms (Ω)

It says: the voltage is the current times the resistance.

The letter on its own on one side is the **subject**. Here it is $V$, so the formula hands you $V$ straight away. If you know $V$ and $R$ and want $I$, you **change the subject**: turn the formula round so $I$ is on its own.

Numbers show how: $12 = 3 \times 4$ also means $12 \div 4 = 3$. So $V = IR$ also means $I = \frac{V}{R}$.
cards.more:
Think of a 'fact family' from school: $3 \times 4 = 12$, $4 \times 3 = 12$, $12 \div 4 = 3$, $12 \div 3 = 4$. Four ways of writing one fact.

A formula is a fact about letters, so it has a family too. $V = IR$, $I = \frac{V}{R}$ and $R = \frac{V}{I}$ are the same rule written three ways. Each has a different subject, and you pick the one whose subject is the thing you want.

Worked number: a lamp on a 24 V supply has a resistance of 48 Ω. You want the current, so use the version with $I$ as the subject: $I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{24}{48} = 0.5$ A. Check it the other way: $0.5 \times 48 = 24$ V. Right.

cards.q: Ohm's law is $V = IR$. Which formula gives the resistance $R$?
cards.why: Numbers: $12 = 3 \times 4$, so $4 = \frac{12}{3}$: the voltage divided by the current. So $R = \frac{V}{I}$. $R = VI$ multiplies instead of dividing. $\frac{I}{V}$ is upside down: 3 A and 12 V would give 0.25 Ω instead of 4 Ω.

cards.title: Undo what was done to the letter
cards.body:
To change the subject, look at what was done to the letter you want. Then **undo** it, doing the **same to both sides**, just as with equations.

The opposites: add and take away; times and divide; square and square root.

Speed is $v = \frac{d}{t}$: the speed $v$ (metres per second, m/s) is the distance $d$ (metres) divided by the time $t$ (seconds).

To get $d$: $d$ was **divided by** $t$, so **multiply** both sides by $t$:

$$d = vt$$

Numbers: 100 m in 20 s is $100 \div 20 = 5$ m/s. And $5 \times 20 = 100$ m back again.
cards.more:
Changing the subject is solving an equation with letters instead of numbers. The moves are the same.

With numbers: $5 = \frac{d}{20}$. Something divided by 20 is 5. Multiply both sides by 20: $d = 100$.

With letters: $v = \frac{d}{t}$. Multiply both sides by $t$: $vt = d$. Swap the sides so the subject is on the left: $d = vt$. (A formula means the same either way round, as $12 = 3 \times 4$ and $3 \times 4 = 12$ do.)

Worked number: a conveyor runs at 0.4 m/s for 30 s. $d = vt = 0.4 \times 30 = 12$ m of belt has gone past.

cards.q: A conveyor belt runs at {v} m/s. How far does a box on it travel in {t} s? Start from $v = \frac{ d }{ t }$ and turn it round for the distance.
cards.why: $d$ was divided by $t$, so multiply both sides by $t$: $d = vt$. Dividing ({v} ÷ {t}) is the slip: a box that rides for longer goes further, so the answer must grow with the time.

cards.title: When the letter is on the bottom
cards.body:
From $v = \frac{d}{t}$, how long does a journey take? Now $t$ is on the **bottom** of the fraction.

Get it off the bottom first: multiply both sides by $t$.

$$vt = d$$

Now $t$ is multiplied by $v$, so divide both sides by $v$:

$$t = \frac{d}{v}$$

Numbers: 100 m at 5 m/s takes $100 \div 5 = 20$ s.

The same two moves turn $I = \frac{V}{R}$ into $R = \frac{V}{I}$.
cards.more:
A letter on the bottom of a fraction is awkward to reach, so bring it up first. Multiplying both sides by it cancels it from the bottom: $\frac{d}{t} \times t$ is just $d$, as $\frac{100}{20} \times 20 = 100$.

Then it is an ordinary times, undone by dividing.

Worked number: a forklift covers 60 m at 1.5 m/s. How long does it take? $t = \frac{d}{v} = \frac{60}{1.5} = 40$ s. Check with the original: $\frac{60}{40} = 1.5$ m/s. Right.

A handy test for any rearranged formula: does it make sense? Further to go, longer time: $d$ on top. Faster, shorter time: $v$ on the bottom.

cards.q: A conveyor runs at {v} m/s. How long does a box take to travel {d} m along it?
cards.hint: Start from $v = \frac{ d }{ t }$. Get $t$ off the bottom first.
cards.why: Multiply both sides by $t$ ($vt = d$), then divide both sides by $v$: $t = \frac{ d }{ v }$. Multiplying {d} by {v} would give a time that grows when the belt runs faster, which cannot be right.

cards.title: Two jobs to undo: the pulse-echo rule
cards.body:
In ultrasonic testing the depth of a flaw is

$$d = \frac{vt}{2}$$

$d$ is the depth, $v$ the speed of sound in the metal and $t$ the time for the echo to come back. It says: speed times time, **halved**, because the sound goes there and back.

To get $t$, list what was done to it: **times $v$**, then **divide by 2**. Undo in reverse:

- times both sides by 2: $2d = vt$
- divide both sides by $v$: $t = \frac{2d}{v}$

For the speed instead: $v = \frac{2d}{t}$. That is how a flaw detector is set up on a block of known thickness.
cards.more:
Numbers first. Steel carries sound at about 5.92 mm per microsecond (µs, a millionth of a second). A flaw 29.6 mm deep: the sound goes down and back, $2 \times 29.6 = 59.2$ mm, which takes $59.2 \div 5.92 = 10$ µs. That is $t = \frac{2d}{v}$.

You can see the order by going forwards and back. Forwards from $t = 10$: times $v$ gives 59.2, divide by 2 gives 29.6. Backwards from 29.6: times 2 gives 59.2, divide by $v$ gives 10. Each step undoes its partner, last first.

For calibration: a 25 mm block echoes at 8.45 µs. $v = \frac{2d}{t} = \frac{50}{8.45} \approx 5.92$ mm per µs.

cards.q: Start from $d = \frac{vt}{2}$. Which gives the speed $v$?
cards.why: Times both sides by 2: $2d = vt$. Divide both sides by $t$: $v = \frac{2d}{t}$. $\frac{d}{2t}$ halves again instead of undoing the halving; that is the usual slip. Check: 29.6 mm and 10 µs give $\frac{59.2}{10} = 5.92$.

cards.title: Squares and square roots
cards.body:
$I^2$ means $I \times I$, the current **squared**. A **square root** undoes it: $4^2 = 16$ and $\sqrt{16} = 4$.

The power turned to heat in a resistor is

$$P = I^2R$$

$P$ is the power (watts, W), $I$ the current (A), $R$ the resistance (Ω). It says: the current squared, times the resistance.

To get $I$: it was squared, then multiplied by $R$. Undo in reverse: divide by $R$, then square root.

$$I = \sqrt{\frac{P}{R}}$$

The area $A$ of a circle of radius $r$ (centre to edge) is $A = \pi r^2$. It turns round the same way: $r = \sqrt{\frac{A}{\pi}}$.
cards.more:
Squaring and square-rooting are opposites, like times and divide. $5^2 = 25$ and $\sqrt{25} = 5$.

Why divide by $R$ **before** the square root? Because in $I^2R$ the squaring was done first and the times $R$ last. Undo the last job first.

Worked number: a 4 Ω resistor turns 100 W into heat. $I^2 = \frac{100}{4} = 25$, so $I = \sqrt{25} = 5$ A. Check: $5^2 \times 4 = 25 \times 4 = 100$ W. Right.

A square root is often a decimal: $\sqrt{50} \approx 7.07$. With no calculator, type SQRT(50) in the answer box.

cards.q: A heater element of {R} Ω turns {P} W into heat. $P = I^2R$. What current flows through it?
cards.hint: Divide by $R$ first, then take the square root.
cards.why: Undo in reverse: $I$ was squared, then multiplied by $R$. So divide by $R$ (giving {k2}), then square root ({answer} A). Square-rooting {P} first and then dividing by {R} undoes the jobs in the wrong order and gives the wrong current.

cards.title: Formulas with brackets
cards.body:
To turn a temperature $C$ in degrees Celsius (°C) into $F$ in degrees Fahrenheit (°F):

$$F = \frac{9C}{5} + 32$$

It says: times by 9, divide by 5, then add 32. Water boils at 100 °C: $900 \div 5 + 32 = 212$ °F.

To get $C$, undo in reverse:

- take 32 from both sides: $F - 32 = \frac{9C}{5}$
- times both sides by 5: $5(F - 32) = 9C$
- divide both sides by 9: $C = \frac{5(F - 32)}{9}$

The **bracket** says: take 32 off first, then multiply the whole result by 5. Check: $(212 - 32) \times 5 \div 9 = 100$.
cards.more:
Why the bracket? Without it, $5F - 32$ would mean 'times $F$ by 5, then take 32': a different order and a different answer. The bracket keeps $F - 32$ together as one amount, so the 5 multiplies all of it.

Worked number: a datasheet gives 176 °F. $176 - 32 = 144$. $144 \times 5 = 720$. $720 \div 9 = 80$ °C.

The pattern for any formula: write down the jobs done to your letter, in order (here: times 9, divide by 5, add 32). Then undo them from the end (take 32, times 5, divide by 9).

cards.q: A pump datasheet gives a fluid temperature of {F} °F. What is that in °C? Start from $F = \frac{9C}{5} + 32$.
cards.hint: What was done last in the formula? Undo that first.
cards.why: Undo in reverse: take 32 off first ({F} − 32 = {f32}), then times by 5, then divide by 9. Taking the 32 off at the end instead gives the wrong answer: it was added last, so it must come off first.

cards.q: A round bar has a cross-section area of 314 mm². What is its radius? Use $A = \pi r^2$.

steps.ask: What was done to $r$, in order?
steps.show: It was squared, then multiplied by $\pi$.

steps.ask: Undo the times $\pi$: divide both sides by $\pi$.
Undo the square: square root both sides.

cards.why: Rearrange first, then put the numbers in: the letters show you the order of the jobs. Square-rooting 314 before dividing by $\pi$ undoes the jobs in the wrong order.

cards.q: A 50 Ω resistor must not turn more than 2 W into heat. What is the largest current it can take? Use $P = I^2R$.

steps.ask: What was done to $I$, in order?
steps.show: It was squared, then multiplied by $R$.
$I = \sqrt{0.04} = 0.2$ A, which is 200 mA (milliamps: thousandths of an amp).

cards.why: The same order as the circle: divide, then square root. $\sqrt{0.04}$ is 0.2 because $0.2 \times 0.2 = 0.04$.

cards.q: A round shaft has a cross-section area of {A} mm². What is its radius? ($A = \pi r^2$.)
cards.hint: Divide by $\pi$ first, then square root. You can type SQRT({A}/PI()).
cards.why: $r$ was squared, then multiplied by $\pi$. Undo in reverse: divide by $\pi$, then square root. Halving instead of square-rooting is a common slip: a square root is not a half.

cards.q: A solenoid coil on a {V} V supply draws {I} A. What is its resistance? ($V = IR$.)
cards.why: $R$ was multiplied by $I$, so divide both sides by $I$: $R = \frac{ V }{ I }$. Multiplying ({V} × {I}) gives the power in watts, not the resistance.

cards.q: Electrical power is $P = VI$: the power $P$ (watts) is the voltage $V$ (volts) times the current $I$ (amps). A {P} W heater runs on 230 V. What current does it draw?
cards.why: $I$ is multiplied by $V$, so divide both sides by $V$: $I = \frac{ P }{ V }$. Dividing the other way, $\frac{230}{{P}}$, gives a current that falls as the heater gets more powerful, which cannot be right.

cards.intro: Two resistors in **series**: one after the other, so the current has one path through both. The total resistance is $R_1 + R_2$ (the small 1 and 2 just label the two resistors). Set the battery and the resistors as you like.

ask.q: Work out the current from the battery, in amps, with $I = \frac{ V }{ R }$ and the total resistance. Then check it against the reading.
ask.why: Total resistance: {R1} + {R2} = {Rt} Ω. $I = \frac{ V }{ R } = \frac{{V}}{{Rt}} = {I}$ A. If the reading is in milliamps (mA), divide by 1000 for amps. Using one resistor on its own gives too big a current: the current has to get through both.

cards.q: Steel carries sound at 5.92 mm per µs. A flaw is {d} mm deep. How long after the pulse does its echo come back? ($d = \frac{vt}{2}$.)
cards.hint: Undo the halving first, then the times $v$.
cards.why: Rearranged: $t = \frac{2d}{v}$. The sound goes down and back, {d} mm each way. Forgetting the 2 gives half the time: the one-way trip only.

cards.q: To make $I$ the subject of $P = I^2R$, why do you divide by $R$ **before** taking the square root?
options: Dividing always comes before square roots
It does not matter which you do first
Undo the last job first: × $R$ was done last
cards.why: Undo in reverse order, as you take off boots before socks. $I$ was squared, then multiplied by $R$, so the times $R$ comes off first. It does matter: with $P = 100$ and $R = 4$, $\sqrt{100} \div 4 = 2.5$, but the right answer is $\sqrt{100 \div 4} = \sqrt{25} = 5$ A. And there is no 'always' rule about dividing: it depends on the order the jobs were done.

cards.q: Put the steps in order to make $C$ the subject of $F = \frac{9C}{5} + 32$.
items: Check with a pair you know: 212 °F should give 100 °C
cards.why: Undo in reverse: the add 32 was the last job, so it comes off first; then undo the divide by 5; then the times 9. A check with numbers you know catches slips.

cards.q: Ohm's law, $V = IR$. Which question can you answer by putting the numbers straight in, **without** rearranging?
options: A 12 V supply drives 0.5 A. What is the resistance?
A 12 V supply is across 24 Ω. What is the current?
A 9 V battery drives 3 A. What is the resistance?
A 0.5 A current flows through 220 Ω. What is the voltage?
cards.why: $V$ is already the subject, so when you want $V$, just substitute: $0.5 \times 220 = 110$ V. The others want $I$ or $R$, so turn the formula round first: $I = \frac{V}{R}$ or $R = \frac{V}{I}$. Ask first: is the letter I want already on its own?

cards.q: Pay is $P = rh$: the hourly rate $r$ (£ an hour) times the hours $h$. You were paid £{p:2} for {h} hours. What was your hourly rate?
cards.why: Rearrange first: $r$ is multiplied by $h$, so divide both sides by $h$. It is the same move as $R = \frac{V}{I}$: 'this = that times that' turns round the same way whatever the letters.

cards.q: $P = I^2R$. The current is 3 A and the resistance 10 Ω. What is the power?
cards.why: Only $I$ is squared: $3^2 = 9$, then $9 \times 10 = 90$ W. 900 W squares $I$ and $R$ together, $(3 \times 10)^2$; 60 W doubles the 3 instead of squaring it. This one is substituting, not rearranging: $P$ is already the subject.

cards.q: Electrical power is $P = VI$ (watts = volts × amps). Which formula gives the current $I$?
cards.why: $I$ is multiplied by $V$, so divide both sides by $V$: $I = \frac{P}{V}$. Check: 2300 W on 230 V is $\frac{2300}{230} = 10$ A, and $230 \times 10 = 2300$. $\frac{V}{P}$ is upside down, and $PV$ multiplies when you should divide.

cards.q: A steel calibration block is {d} mm thick. Its back-wall echo comes back at {t} µs. Find the speed of sound, in mm per µs. ($d = \frac{vt}{2}$.)
cards.hint: Undo the halving, then divide by $t$.
cards.why: Rearranged for the speed: times both sides by 2, then divide by $t$, so $v = \frac{2d}{ t }$. Leaving out the 2 gives half the real speed, because the echo time is there and back.

cards.q: Match each formula to the same formula rearranged for the letter shown.
cards.why: Undo in reverse order each time: a letter on the bottom comes up first; the square root comes after dividing; the halving is undone by doubling.
